touches.text: The ticket IS its own manager. It carries its workflow and status, and asks each gate whether it can transit. If refused, it gets itself back to design for fixing. If no handler is available to ask, it throws a trouble and waits until we decide. Design is CC and Akien. Akien, 2026-11-11, Q#85: "you and me. later there will be a specific agent for it, but that's so far off we're not even thinking about it now except 'after the outline is implemented'." So until then a refused ticket waits in the trouble lane, which both of us read when a session opens, and nothing posts to a design verb that no machine answers.
The ticket owns its refusals: a gate refuses a crossing on the ticket's behalf. The gates are CodeMother's (9.3.5).

The workflow drives it. When a step's work is finished, the ticket asks that step's gate. Once the gate passes, its post-gate probes send mail over the bus to every device that can do the next step, naming the step (BUILDME, PROVEME, ...), and a device comes to claim it. A builder never goes looking for what's next: it gets the mail and does that. When several compete, the least capable one that thinks it can do it claims it, "leaving the more capable in case a bigger one comes along."
Commit often. WHY: so we never wind up with stray files or incomplete work.

More than one builder runs at a time, so work is kept apart by branches: each ticket's work on its own branch, named by the ticket id, merged locally with git, no pull request (GitHub is hosting only). WHY: "the best way to manage scaling is branches."
Owns the inspectors and gates (9.4): everything in the code pipeline that checks. The exception is diagnostic_inspector, which is base's (17.1).
It outputs only its findings. It certifies nothing, records no crossing, and posts nothing; the gate consumes its findings.

It is the READY TO MERGE ONTO MAIN step of the pipeline: everything's proved, and merging implies pushing it up. With a branch per ticket (3.3.6), commits on the branch are as often as we like; the inspector is the step at ready to merge. Checking what a change touched belongs here; nothing hangs off the git post-commit hook.

Once build_inspector moves into CodeMother, code outside her reaches it over the bus: the 18 crossing calls in transitions.py, the other code sites and the 82 proofs that run a sieve over themselves. No published client tool, no fifth exception. Akien 2026-11-13, on Q#88: "over the bus. that's what it's for?"

A rule not yet enforced is made into a ticket now. Akien 2026-11-13, on Q#89: "i said no ious because you were making a lot of them. ious have to be made into tickets. if we have them floating around, then they need to be made tickets NOW." So ticket f5dbfddea8c6 makes the rewrites it proposed at the 24 remaining sites (CLAUDE.md, MAP.md, the press office, PROOF.md). Where a site names a rule whose physics is not built, it names that rule's real ticket id, cast now if none exists; the word "ticket" with no id behind it does not count. CC's reading of his answer, on a mechanism CC made.

Reds don't get lost. Each run writes a ticket for every new red it finds and every orphaned file it sees, unless one is already open for it. A red seen in passing gets the same treatment. Akien 2026-11-13: "every test failure, every orphaned file, HAS TO BE FIXED. if we get 3 reds but they're really not related to what we just did, we can ticket them for fixing. reds don't get lost." and "so each run writes any new bugs". Once a red unrelated to a crossing is ticketed, that crossing can go ahead.
